body:
Conservation beyond forests and national parks

Biodiversity includes the variety of living organisms and their relationships with one another and the environment. Important biological resources also occur outside protected forests: in farmland, village commons, wetlands, coastal areas, urban green spaces and traditional community-managed landscapes.

The Biological Diversity Act, 2002, as amended in 2023, establishes an institutional framework for conservation, sustainable use of biodiversity and fair and equitable sharing of benefits arising from the use of biological resources and associated knowledge.

The national, state and local institutions

National Biodiversity Authority

The National Biodiversity Authority (NBA) carries out national-level regulatory, advisory and related functions under the Biological Diversity Act. It deals with specified access-related matters according to the Act.

Gujarat Biodiversity Board

The Gujarat Biodiversity Board is Gujarat's state-level institution under this framework. It supports biodiversity conservation and performs the state-board functions assigned by law, including relevant advice and regulation concerning biological resources.

Biodiversity Management Committees

Biodiversity Management Committees (BMCs) are constituted by local bodies under Section 41 of the Biological Diversity Act. They support conservation, sustainable use and documentation of local biodiversity.

A major responsibility is the preparation and maintenance of the People's Biodiversity Register (PBR). A PBR records locally relevant biological resources and associated knowledge. It is a biodiversity-documentation instrument, not a general building permit or an industrial pollution consent.

The Biological Diversity Rules, 2024, came into force in December 2024 and were subsequently amended in 2025. The precise rules on access and benefit sharing must therefore be read with the amended legal framework rather than assumed from older notes.

Municipalities and panchayats

Urban local bodies, including municipal corporations and municipalities, and rural local bodies, including panchayats, carry out important environmental functions through local administration. Depending on the applicable state laws, their duties include sanitation, public cleanliness, drainage, waste collection and provision or management of related civic facilities.

These responsibilities concern services delivered to residents. They differ from GPCB's statutory power to regulate pollution under the Water and Air Acts. A municipality may operate a sewage-treatment facility, while that facility may separately be subject to pollution-control requirements.

Solid Waste Management Rules, 2026

The Solid Waste Management Rules, 2026, notified through S.O. 388(E), dated 27 January 2026, came into force on 1 April 2026. They superseded the Solid Waste Management Rules, 2016, subject to the legal savings stated in the notification.

The 2026 rules assign responsibilities to urban and rural local bodies, waste generators, processing and disposal facilities, pollution-control boards and other institutions. A central requirement is segregation of municipal solid waste at source into 4 streams:

  • Wet waste: Biodegradable waste such as food and vegetable remains.
  • Dry waste: Materials such as paper, plastic, metals and glass.
  • Sanitary waste: Specified personal-hygiene waste requiring separate handling.
  • Special care waste: Specified household items requiring particular care, such as discarded medicines, bulbs and paint containers.

Local bodies organise collection and transport and support suitable processing and disposal arrangements. GPCB has separate monitoring and regulatory responsibilities under the relevant rules. The 2026 framework also establishes responsibilities for covered bulk waste generators.

GIDC and other state organisations

GIDC develops and manages industrial infrastructure, including industrial estates and certain common facilities. Its functions are developmental and infrastructural rather than a general power to grant every environmental clearance.

The Gujarat Ecology Commission has functions related to environmental assessment, information and ecological initiatives, including work on the State of Environment Report. It should not be confused with GPCB's statutory pollution-consent role.

Prelims focus

  • Biological Diversity Act: 2002; important amendment: 2023.
  • NBA: national institution; Gujarat Biodiversity Board: state institution.
  • Section 41: local Biodiversity Management Committees and their biodiversity-related functions.
  • PBR means People's Biodiversity Register.
  • Solid Waste Management Rules, 2026, came into force on 1 April 2026.
  • Trap: Local waste-service responsibilities do not make a municipality the state pollution control board.

[Sources: Biological Diversity Act, 2002, as amended by the Biological Diversity (Amendment) Act, 2023, especially Section 41; National Biodiversity Authority, official FAQs, sections on institutional responsibilities and the 2024 and 2025 rules; MoEFCC, Solid Waste Management Rules, 2026, S.O. 388(E), 27 January 2026; CPCB, Centralised Online Portal for Solid Waste Management, Rules 2026 overview; NCERT, Social and Political Life I, Class 6, Chapters 5–7, Panchayati Raj, Rural Administration and Urban Administration; NCERT, Social and Political Life III, Class 8, Chapter 9, Public Facilities; Government of Gujarat, Forests and Environment Department, resolution concerning State of Environment reporting, 22 November 2022. Official sources consulted 1 November 2026.]

title: Biodiversity Institutions and Local Environmental Governance in Gujarat

body:
Start with the activity and the location

To determine which environmental institutions are relevant to a proposed development in Gujarat, examine what the project will do and where it will operate. These are separate questions. An activity may create industrial emissions without affecting a forest, or it may affect a sensitive coastal habitat while producing very little routine air pollution.

Example 1: A manufacturing unit in an industrial estate

Suppose an entrepreneur proposes a chemical-processing unit in a Gujarat industrial estate.

  1. Identify the activity: Determine its official industrial category and whether its process requires GPCB operating consent and applicable waste authorisation.
  2. Check the EIA Schedule: If the specific activity meets the conditions for prior EC, determine whether central or state appraisal applies.
  3. Apply the current CTE rules: If it requires and obtains EC, the November 2024 exemption removes the separate CTE requirement under the Water and Air Acts. If no such exemption applies, determine whether CTE is required. A genuinely covered White-category activity follows its separate exemption and intimation rules.
  4. Prepare for operation: Obtain CTO where required, ensure treatment equipment functions and comply with emission, wastewater and waste-management conditions.
  5. Check additional permissions: Land-use, building, fire-safety, groundwater and other statutory requirements may apply independently.

If the estate has a common effluent treatment plant, the unit must still comply with applicable inlet and discharge conditions. Infrastructure availability is not the same as proof of legal compliance.

Example 2: A proposed facility near a coastal port

Now consider a facility proposed near the Gulf of Kachchh. Its exact coordinates and the approved Coastal Zone Management Plan must first be examined. The fact that a district is coastal does not automatically establish that every plot in the district falls inside a regulated CRZ area.

If the plot falls within CRZ, the proposed activity must be tested against the restrictions applicable to that zone. GCZMA performs its designated scrutiny and recommendation functions. The competent authority handles the applicable clearance decision.

Other obligations may arise simultaneously: an EIA-listed project may require prior EC; an industrial facility may require GPCB consent; and a project affecting the Marine National Park or applicable forest land may require separate wildlife or forest consideration. One approval cannot be assumed to replace the others.

Example 3: A municipality planning a solid-waste facility

A Gujarat municipality organising a waste-processing facility acts in its capacity as a local body responsible for waste services. It must follow the Solid Waste Management Rules, 2026, including duties concerning segregation, collection and environmentally sound management.

The facility may also be subject to applicable registration, authorisation, consent or other environmental requirements. Whether a separate prior EC is needed depends on whether the proposed activity falls within the applicable EIA Schedule; it should not be presumed merely because the municipality is building infrastructure.

A practical distinction between the authorities

Main questionRelevant institutionDecision or responsibility
Will the activity cause regulated pollution?GPCBApplicable consent, standards, monitoring and enforcement
Is the project listed for prior EC?MoEFCC/EAC or SEIAA/SEACEnvironmental appraisal and EC decision
Is the site inside regulated coastal land or waters?GCZMA and competent clearance authorityCRZ scrutiny and applicable permission
Does the project require covered forest-land diversion?Forest administration and Central GovernmentForest scrutiny and applicable central prior approval
Does it affect a protected wildlife area?Competent wildlife authoritiesWildlife-related statutory scrutiny and permissions
Who delivers municipal waste services?Urban or rural local bodyLocal collection, processing arrangements and civic duties

Compliance continues after approval

Environmental permission is conditional. The operator must comply with its terms throughout the relevant activity, maintain prescribed controls and obtain further approval when legally required for changes. The competent regulator may inspect and take action against violations under the relevant law.

For a prelims question, first identify whether the statement concerns pollution, project appraisal, coastal location, forest land, wildlife protection, biodiversity documentation or local sanitation. Then match it to the institution and legal requirement. This approach avoids confusing authorities simply because they all work in environmental protection.

Prelims focus

  • GPCB consent is distinct from EIA environmental clearance.
  • SEAC makes expert recommendations; SEIAA decides applicable state-level EC.
  • CRZ applicability depends on the regulated location and approved coastal-management plan.
  • Covered forest-land diversion needs prior Central Government approval.
  • Municipal waste duties operate under the Solid Waste Management Rules, 2026.
  • Trap: Industrial-estate infrastructure, local building approval or one environmental permission does not automatically replace every other applicable approval.

[Sources: MoEFCC, EIA Notification, S.O. 1533(E), 14 September 2006, paragraphs 2–7 and Schedule; MoEFCC, G.S.R. 702(E) and 703(E), 12 November 2024, and Lok Sabha clarification, 3 February 2025; MoEFCC, CRZ Notification, G.S.R. 37(E), 18 January 2019; Gazette of India, S.O. 713(E), 11 February 2026, GCZMA functions; Van (Sanrakshan Evam Samvardhan) Adhiniyam, 1980, Section 2; MoEFCC, Solid Waste Management Rules, 2026, S.O. 388(E); GIDC, official industrial-estate guidance. Official sources consulted 1 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Three overlapping checks for a Gujarat project connect activities, location and civic duties to relevant authorities, followed by continuing compliance.
pictures.caption: A Gujarat project may face several independent environmental checks.
